title: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline
summary: Rendering turns the game's state into pixels, mostly on the **GPU**. This lesson follows a frame from the CPU's side (what to draw, culling, sorting, **draw calls**) through the GPU's pipeline (**vertex shaders**, **rasterisation**, **pixel shaders**, depth testing) to the screen, with the coordinate transforms in between. It is a map for the graphics work in chapter 11 and beyond.
markdown:
## The CPU and the GPU The **GPU** is a separate processor with thousands of simple cores, built to run the same small program on huge numbers of vertices and pixels in parallel. The CPU does not draw pixels; it prepares work for the GPU and submits it through a graphics API: **Direct3D 11/12** on Windows, **Vulkan**, **OpenGL**, or **Metal** on Apple systems. Libraries like SDL and raylib (chapter 11) sit on top of these. ```mermaid flowchart LR G["Game state
(CPU)"] --> V["Visibility
culling, sorting"] V --> D["Draw calls
+ buffers, textures, shaders"] D --> VS["Vertex shader
(GPU)"] VS --> RA["Rasterisation"] RA --> PS["Pixel shader"] PS --> OM["Depth test, blending
into the back buffer"] OM --> P["Present
swap to the screen"] ``` ## The CPU's part Each frame the renderer: 1. **Collects** what might be visible: sprites, models, particles, interface. 2. **Culls**: skips everything outside the camera's view (a rectangle in 2D, a pyramid-shaped **frustum** in 3D). Cheap bounding-box tests remove most objects before any GPU work. The practice task does this for 2D. 3. **Sorts**: transparent objects back to front (so blending is correct); opaque objects by material or texture, to minimise state changes. 4. **Submits draw calls**: each tells the GPU "draw these triangles with this shader, these textures and these settings". Draw calls have a CPU cost of their own. Drawing ten thousand sprites as ten thousand separate calls is slow; **batching** them (many sprites sharing a texture atlas in one call) or **instancing** (one model drawn many times in one call) is how games draw large scenes. ## Coordinates and transforms Positions pass through several coordinate systems on the way to the screen: | Space | Meaning | |---|---| | **Model (local) space** | Relative to the object itself: a character model's feet at (0, 0, 0) | | **World space** | Where it is in the level (the scene graph of lesson 3.09 combines these) | | **View (camera) space** | Relative to the camera | | **Clip space / NDC** | After projection: what lies inside the view becomes the range −1 to 1 | | **Screen space** | Pixels on the render target | Each step is a matrix multiplication, combined into one matrix per object and applied to every vertex by the vertex shader. In 2D the idea is the same with simpler maths: subtract the camera's position, multiply by the zoom, and add half the screen size to put the camera's centre in the middle. ## The GPU's part - **Vertex shader**: a small program run once per vertex, transforming its position into clip space and passing along data such as texture coordinates and colours. - **Rasterisation**: fixed hardware works out which pixels each triangle covers and interpolates the vertex data across them. - **Pixel (fragment) shader**: run once per covered pixel, computing its colour: sampling textures, applying lighting. - **Output merging**: the **depth test** discards pixels behind something already drawn (using the depth buffer); **blending** combines transparent pixels with what is behind them. Shaders are written in their own languages (HLSL for Direct3D, GLSL for OpenGL and Vulkan) and compiled for the GPU. ## Buffers and presenting The GPU draws into a **back buffer** while the monitor shows the **front buffer**; at the end of the frame they are swapped (**present**), the same idea as lesson 5.06's double buffering. With vsync, the swap waits for the monitor's refresh (lesson 10.02). ## Where the time goes | Bottleneck | Symptom | Typical fix | |---|---|---| | CPU: too many draw calls | GPU often idle; CPU busy in the renderer | Batching, instancing, fewer state changes | | GPU: too many pixels (fill rate) | Slower at higher resolutions; heavy effects | Cheaper pixel shaders, lower resolution effects, less overdraw | | GPU: too many vertices | Slower with detailed models regardless of resolution | Level of detail (simpler models far away) | | Transfers | Stalls when uploading textures mid-game | Upload during loading, or asynchronously | GPU profilers (PIX for Direct3D, RenderDoc for most APIs, vendor tools) show where a frame's GPU time goes, like lesson 8.08's CPU profiling. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] One draw call per sprite > Batch sprites that share a texture, or use an atlas. > [!warning] Reading back from the GPU every frame > The CPU waits for the GPU to finish. Avoid it, or read results a frame or two later. > [!warning] Drawing everything without culling > Off-screen objects still cost CPU and GPU time. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What are the main stages a triangle goes through on the GPU? + Vertex shader, rasterisation, pixel shader, then output merging - Rasterisation, vertex shader, culling, then presenting - The pixel shader runs first, then the vertex shader positions the result - The CPU colours the pixels and the GPU only copies them to the screen > The depth test in output merging decides which surface is in front at each pixel. ? What coordinate spaces does a vertex pass through? - Screen space, then world space, then model space - World space only, which the GPU draws directly + Model, world, view, clip and screen space - Texture space, model space and screen space > Each step is a transform: placing the model in the world, seeing it from the camera, projecting it, then mapping to pixels. ? What is the difference between being CPU-bound and GPU-bound in rendering? - CPU-bound means the game uses too much memory; GPU-bound means it uses too little - They mean the same thing in different engines + CPU-bound: submitting work is too slow; GPU-bound: drawing it is - CPU-bound happens only on laptops; GPU-bound only on desktops > Too many draw calls is a typical cause of being CPU-bound, which is why batching helps. ? What does a vertex shader do? - Runs once per pixel to compute its colour + Transforms each vertex's position for rasterisation - Sorts the objects in the scene > Pixel shaders compute colours; vertex shaders place vertices. ? Why batch many sprites into one draw call? - The GPU can only draw one call per frame - Batching makes the sprites sharper + Each draw call costs CPU time, so fewer is faster > Submission overhead adds up with thousands of calls. ? What does the depth test do? + Discards pixels that are behind something already drawn at that position - Measures how far the camera is from the scene - Sorts transparent objects > It uses the depth buffer, one depth value per pixel. ? What is culling? - Removing objects from the game + Skipping objects that cannot be seen - Compressing textures > Cheap tests save expensive drawing. ```
ideas:
- Download RenderDoc, capture a frame of any OpenGL, Vulkan or Direct3D 11 program of your own, and look at its draw calls in order.
- Work out by hand which of five rectangles are visible to a camera, using the practice task's rules.
- Count how many draw calls lesson 5.06's GDI program makes per frame, and think about how a GPU renderer would batch them.
